teile.einleitung: A graphics processing unit, GPU for short, is a special computer chip that calculates images, videos and 3D graphics. It makes sure video games run smoothly and films appear sharp on the screen. Today it is also one of the most important machines for artificial intelligence.
wichtigste: GPU stands for graphics processing unit.
The main job of a graphics processor is calculating images and 3D graphics.
It has very many small processing cores that work in parallel.
A graphics card's own memory is called graphics memory or VRAM.
A graphics processor colours in the individual picture dots, the pixels.
60 fps means that 60 frames are shown per second.
Integrated graphics are built into the main processor.
Powerful GPUs are often used today to train artificial intelligence.

abschnitte.text: GPU is short for **graphics processing unit**, in German “Grafikprozessor”. Besides the main processor, the **CPU**, it is one of the most important chips in a computer. Its main job is to calculate images and 3D graphics. It sits either on its own **graphics card** or is built into the main processor. Mobile phones, games consoles and cars also have graphics processors.

A main processor has only a few processing cores, but they are very versatile. A graphics processor, on the other hand, has thousands of small **processing cores** that all work at the same time. This is called **parallel processing**. You can imagine it like a whole school class solving simple sums at the same time, instead of a single maths genius. For many similar calculations this is much faster.

A screen is made up of millions of tiny picture dots, the **pixels**. The graphics processor calculates what colour each pixel should be, with light, shadows and reflections. In a video game it has to do this many times per second. The figure **60 fps** means that 60 frames are shown per second. The higher the frame rate, the smoother the game looks.

A graphics card has its own fast memory, the **graphics memory** or VRAM. This holds, for example, the textures, that is, the surface images of characters and landscapes. Many laptops have no graphics card of their own but **integrated graphics**. This graphics part is built into the main processor; it uses less electricity but is usually less powerful. It is quite enough for office work and videos.

Because graphics processors can manage so many calculations at the same time, they are now also used for other tasks. They are especially important for training **artificial intelligence**, for which huge data centres with thousands of GPUs are built. Researchers also use them for weather forecasts or simulations. Well-known makers of graphics processors are Nvidia, AMD and Intel.

In the past the main processor calculated the images all by itself. In the 1990s special **3D accelerators** for computer games came onto the market. In 1999 the company Nvidia advertised its GeForce 256 as the first GPU. Since then graphics processors have become many times more powerful.

begriffe.erklaerung: Abbreviation for graphics processing unit.
Single picture dot on a screen.
Frames per second.
Separate fast memory on a graphics card.
Many calculations are done at the same time instead of one after another.

gewusst: A modern graphics processor has thousands of processing cores, while a main processor often has only a handful to a few dozen.
Many artificial intelligence programs are trained on graphics processors that were originally invented for games.
A 4K screen has over eight million pixels, which the graphics processor can recalculate for every frame.

teile.einleitung: A lever is a simple machine with which you can move heavy things using little force. It consists of a rigid bar that turns around a pivot. Levers are everywhere in everyday life, from door handles to bike brake levers.
wichtigste: A lever is a rigid bar that turns around a pivot.
The distance from the pivot to the point where the force acts is called the lever arm.
The further from the pivot you push, the less force you need.
In return you have to move a longer distance.
Archimedes is said to have claimed that with a lever he could move the world.
Door handles, bottle openers, crowbars and bike brake levers are levers.
Our arm also works like a lever.

abschnitte.text: A **lever** is a rigid bar that is supported at one point. This point is called the **pivot**. On one side acts the force with which you push or pull, on the other the load you want to move. The distance from the pivot to the force is called the **lever arm**. Together with the wedge, the pulley and the inclined plane, the lever is one of the simple machines.

A simple rule applies to the lever: force times effort arm equals load times load arm. If the effort arm is twice as long as the load arm, you need only half the force. But in return you have to move the end of the lever twice as far. So you save force, but not work. This **law of the lever** was already described by the Greek scholar **Archimedes** more than 2,200 years ago.

A **door handle** is a lever that pulls back the latch in the lock. With a **bottle opener** you lever off a crown cap with no effort. A crowbar helps to lever up heavy things. The brake lever on a bicycle, scissors, pliers and a wheelbarrow also work with levers. In the playground, the seesaw is a large lever with the pivot in the middle.

Our body uses levers too. When you lift a bag, your **forearm** is the lever and your elbow is the pivot. The muscles pull close to the joint, while the load hangs far away in your hand. That is why muscles have to exert much more force than the bag weighs. In return the hand can move quickly and a long way.

Archimedes lived in the 3rd century BC in **Syracuse** in Sicily. The saying “Give me a firm place to stand, and I will lift the world off its hinges” is attributed to him. He wanted to show how powerful a lever with a long arm is. In reality, of course, there would be no place for the pivot and no such long bar. But the ancient Egyptians already used levers to move heavy blocks of stone.

begriffe.erklaerung: The point around which a lever turns.
The distance from the pivot to the force.
Force times effort arm equals load times load arm.
A basic tool that saves force, such as a lever, wedge or pulley.

gewusst: With a crowbar a child can move a stone that they could never lift with their bare hands.
On a seesaw a light child can lift a heavy child if the light child sits further out.
A nutcracker is a lever in which the nut and the hand are on the same side of the pivot.

teile.einleitung: A suspension bridge is a bridge whose deck hangs from thick cables. The cables run over tall towers and are firmly anchored on land. In this way suspension bridges can span huge distances over rivers, bays and gorges.
wichtigste: On a suspension bridge the deck hangs from large main cables.
The main cables are under tension, which means they are pulled apart.
The main cables run over tall towers, the pylons.
The ends of the cables are fixed in heavy anchor blocks on land.
Vertical cables, the hangers, connect the deck with the main cables.
Suspension bridges reach the longest spans of all kinds of bridges.
The longest span belongs to the Çanakkale Bridge in Turkey (as of 2026).

abschnitte.text: A large suspension bridge usually has two tall towers, the **pylons**. The thick **main cables** run over them from one bank to the other. Many vertical cables, the **hangers**, hang down from the main cables. The deck is attached to them. The ends of the main cables are set in huge concrete anchor blocks on land.

The weight of the deck and the cars pulls on the hangers and therefore on the main cables. So the cables are under **tension**. The pylons carry the weight down into the ground, so they are squeezed together. A freely hanging cable forms a **catenary**; under the even load of a deck it becomes roughly a parabola. Because steel cables can withstand a great deal of tension, they can be used to bridge especially long distances.

Long, light bridges can swing in the wind. In 1940 the **Tacoma Narrows Bridge** in the USA collapsed because the wind set it swinging more and more strongly. The disaster was filmed and is still famous today. Since then bridge shapes have been tested in a **wind tunnel**. Modern decks often have a flat, streamlined shape like an aircraft wing.

The **Brooklyn Bridge** in New York opened in 1883 and was one of the first with main cables made of steel wire. The **Golden Gate Bridge** in San Francisco has been a landmark since 1937; its main span is about 1,280 metres. In Japan the Akashi Kaikyō Bridge has spanned a strait since 1998. Today the record is held by the **Çanakkale Bridge** in Turkey, which opened in 2022 and has a free span of over 2,000 metres.

In the Swiss Alps there are many **pedestrian suspension bridges** over gorges and glacier streams. A very well-known one is the Charles Kuonen Suspension Bridge near Randa in Valais, which opened in 2017 and is almost 500 metres long. The Trift Bridge in the Bernese Oberland also attracts many hikers. Such bridges sway a little when you walk across. For big motorways, Switzerland tends to use other kinds of bridges.

begriffe.erklaerung: A tall tower over which the main cables run.
A vertical cable from which the deck hangs.
The free distance between two supports of a bridge.
A heavy concrete block that holds the cable ends in place on land.
A force that pulls something apart.

gewusst: The main cables of the Golden Gate Bridge are made of tens of thousands of thin steel wires bundled together.
The Golden Gate Bridge is not golden but painted in an orange-red colour.
The Incas already built simple suspension bridges from plant fibres in the Andes.

teile.einleitung: The Jaquet-Droz automata are three elaborate figures built in the 18th century in La Chaux-de-Fonds in the Neuchâtel Jura. The Writer, the Draughtsman and the Musician move like living people thanks to thousands of gearwheels and cams. They are considered masterpieces of Swiss watchmaking and early forerunners of the computer.
wichtigste: Pierre and Henri-Louis Jaquet-Droz built the automata with Jean-Frédéric Leschot between 1768 and 1774.
The automata are the Writer, the Draughtsman and the Musician.
The Writer consists of about 6,000 parts.
His text can be set freely using a wheel with exchangeable characters, which is why he is considered a forerunner of the programmable computer.
Among other things, the Draughtsman draws a portrait of King Louis XV of France.
The Musician plays a real organ with her fingers.
The automata served as advertising for their makers' watches at royal courts.
Today they are in the Musée d'art et d'histoire in Neuchâtel.

abschnitte.text: **Pierre Jaquet-Droz** was a watchmaker from La Chaux-de-Fonds in the canton of Neuchâtel. Together with his son **Henri-Louis** and the mechanic Jean-Frédéric Leschot, he built the three automata between 1768 and 1774. At that time the Jura was already a centre of watchmaking. The family wanted to show with the figures how well they could handle the finest mechanics.

The **Writer** is a boy sitting at a desk and writing with a goose quill. He dips the quill in the inkpot, shakes it lightly and follows the text with his eyes. He consists of about 6,000 parts. On a wheel, characters can be exchanged so that he can write a freely chosen text of up to about 40 letters, a kind of **program**.

The **Draughtsman** is also a boy and can draw four different pictures. These include a portrait of King **Louis XV** of France and a little dog. Now and then he blows the dust off his sheet. His movements are controlled by cams, in which the lines are stored like memories.

The **Musician** is a young woman who plays a real small organ. She really presses the keys with her fingers, so the notes do not come from a hidden music box. As she plays, her chest rises and falls as if she were breathing, and she moves her head and eyes. At the end of a piece she bows to the audience.

The Jaquet-Droz family travelled with the automata to kings and princes all over Europe. The audiences were amazed, and many afterwards bought the family's watches. So the automata were brilliant **advertising**. After changing hands many times, they were bought by the city of Neuchâtel at the beginning of the 20th century so that they would stay in Switzerland.

The three figures are now in the **Musée d'art et d'histoire** in Neuchâtel. After more than 250 years they still work and are demonstrated on certain days. Experts see the Writer as an early forerunner of the programmable computer. The automata show how advanced Swiss precision mechanics already was in the 18th century.

begriffe.erklaerung: Machine that carries out a sequence by itself.
Irregularly shaped disc that controls a movement as it turns.
Making very small, precise mechanical parts, as in watches.
Fixed sequence of instructions that a machine carries out.

gewusst: The Writer can be given a new text every time; you only have to exchange the characters on his wheel.
The Musician seems to breathe, because her chest rises and falls while she plays.
The word android for human-like machines was already used at the time of the Jaquet-Droz automata.

teile.einleitung: A hairdryer is an electrical device that blows warm air so that wet hair dries faster. In Switzerland it is usually called a “Föhn”, after the warm downslope wind in the Alps. Today there is one in almost every bathroom.
wichtigste: A hairdryer dries wet hair with a stream of warm air.
In Switzerland it is usually called a “Föhn”.
Inside there is a fan and a heating wire.
A grille at the back stops hair being sucked in.
The cool setting blows cool air and is kind to the hair.
A hairdryer must never fall into water, because there is a risk of electric shock.

abschnitte.text: Inside the casing, a small **electric motor** turns a fan. This sucks in air at the back and blows it out again at the front. In between is a **heating wire**, which glows when electricity flows through it and warms the air. Warm air can take up a lot of water vapour, so the water in the hair evaporates faster.

Most devices have several settings for the strength of the airflow and for the heat. With the **cool setting**, the hairdryer blows cool air so that a hairstyle holds. The narrow attachment at the front is called the **nozzle** and directs the air at one spot. A wide attachment with prongs, the **diffuser**, spreads the air gently and is often used for curls.

Electricity and water together are very dangerous. A hairdryer must therefore never fall into the bath or the washbasin, not even when switched off, as long as it is plugged in. In bathrooms a **residual current device** (RCD) protects against deadly electric shocks by switching off the current in a flash. Built-in overheating protection switches the device off if it gets too hot.

You should not hold the hairdryer right up against your scalp, because the hot air can burn. A distance of about a hand's width is good. Gently drying your hair with a towel first saves time and electricity. Every now and then you should clean dust and hair off the grille at the back so that the device does not overheat.

Around 1890 the Frenchman Alexandre Godefroy developed a large hairdryer for hairdressing salons. Small hand-held devices appeared from the early 20th century. The German company AEG registered the name **Fön** as a trademark. Because the name became so well known, many people still call every hairdryer a “Föhn” today.

begriffe.erklaerung: Warm, dry downslope wind in the Alps, and the Swiss word for a hairdryer.
A wire that gets hot when electricity flows through it.
Wide attachment that spreads the air gently.
Safety switch that cuts off the current immediately if current flows away the wrong way.

gewusst: In German-speaking Switzerland the hairdryer is named after a wind that blows in Swiss valleys such as the Reuss valley or the Rhine valley.
A hairdryer often uses about as much electricity as a kettle.
The first hairdryers in hairdressing salons were so big that you had to sit under a hood.

teile.einleitung: Graphene is a form of carbon that is only a single layer of atoms thick. The atoms in it are arranged like a honeycomb of hexagons. Graphene is extremely thin, very strong and conducts electricity excellently, which is why it is considered a wonder material of the future.
wichtigste: Graphene consists of a single-atom layer of carbon atoms in hexagons.
The carbon atoms are sp² hybridised.
Graphene was first obtained in 2004 by peeling graphite with sticky tape.
Andre Geim and Konstantin Novoselov received the Nobel Prize in Physics for it in 2010.
A single layer of graphene absorbs about 2.3 per cent of visible light.
Ideal graphene has no band gap and a very high electron mobility.
Relative to its thickness, graphene has a record-breaking tensile strength.
Empa makes graphene nanoribbons to create a band gap.

abschnitte.text: Graphene is a special form of the element **carbon**. The atoms form a flat layer made entirely of hexagons, like honeycomb or a chain-link fence. This layer is only a single atom thick, which makes it one of the thinnest materials of all. If you stack many layers of graphene on top of each other, you get **graphite**, the material in pencil leads. So every pencil line contains tiny pieces made of a few layers of graphene.

For a long time people believed such a thin layer could not be stable at all. In 2004 **Andre Geim** and **Konstantin Novoselov** at the University of Manchester succeeded in making graphene. To do this they used **sticky tape** to peel thin layers off a piece of graphite again and again until only a single layer was left. This amazingly simple method made graphene world-famous. In 2010 the two received the Nobel Prize in Physics for it.

Relative to its thickness, graphene is considered one of the strongest materials of all and has an extremely high **tensile strength**. At the same time it is flexible and almost transparent, because one layer absorbs only about 2.3 per cent of visible light. It conducts heat and electricity excellently. The electrons move especially fast in it; this is called high **electron mobility**. The carbon atoms are sp² hybridised, that is, each is joined to three neighbours in one plane.

Ideal graphene has no **band gap**, so it cannot simply be used like silicon as a switch in computer chips. That is why researchers at Empa in Dübendorf make narrow **graphene nanoribbons**. They are built up atom by atom on surfaces through targeted chemical synthesis. Depending on the width and shape of the ribbons, a band gap is created. One day this could make tiny, fast electronic components possible.

Researchers are testing graphene for flexible screens, faster electronics, better batteries and light, stable composite materials. It is already found today in some sports equipment such as tennis rackets or bike helmets. It is also being researched as a filter for water or as a sensor. But making large, flawless sheets of graphene is still difficult and expensive.

begriffe.erklaerung: Chemical element that diamond and graphite are also made of.
Many layers of graphene lying on top of each other, for example in pencil leads.
Energy gap that makes a material a switchable semiconductor.
Very narrow strip of a material, only a few atoms wide.
How hard a material can be pulled before it tears.

gewusst: When you write with a pencil, you create tiny pieces made of a few layers of graphene.
The Nobel Prize for graphene started with an ordinary piece of sticky tape.
Before the Nobel Prize, Andre Geim also received a joke prize for making a frog float with magnets.

teile.einleitung: An insulator is a material or a component that conducts electric current not at all or hardly at all. Insulators protect us from electric shocks and hold high-voltage power lines safely on their pylons. Good insulators are, for example, glass, porcelain, plastic, rubber and dry air.
wichtigste: An insulator hardly conducts electric current at all.
Inside an insulator there are hardly any freely moving charge carriers.
Conductors such as copper, on the other hand, conduct electricity very well.
Overhead lines hang on insulators made of porcelain, glass or plastic.
The bare wires of an overhead line are insulated from each other by the surrounding air.
At very high voltage even air can become conductive, as lightning shows.
Dielectric strength shows up to what voltage an insulating material holds.

abschnitte.text: Electric current is the movement of charged particles, usually **electrons**. In metals such as copper or aluminium many electrons can move freely, which is why they are called **conductors**. In an **insulator** the electrons are tightly bound to their atoms. Because there are hardly any freely moving charge carriers, almost no current flows. In between there are semiconductors such as silicon, which are needed for computer chips.

Every cable in the flat consists of copper wires with a **plastic** coating. The coating means you can touch the cable safely. Plugs and sockets have plastic casings, and electricians wear insulating gloves and use tools with plastic handles. Rubber, glass, ceramics and dry wood also hardly conduct electricity. Water with dissolved substances, on the other hand, does conduct, which is why electrical appliances never belong in the bath.

High-voltage lines in Switzerland carry voltages of up to 380,000 volts. The bare cables hang on long chains of **porcelain**, glass or plastic that separate the cables from the steel pylon. The ribbed shape lengthens the path over the surface so that in rain no current creeps along the wet insulator. Between the cables themselves there is no coating; there the **air** insulates. That is why the cables must hang far enough apart.

Every insulating material only holds up to a certain voltage; this is called **dielectric strength**. If the voltage becomes too great, the insulation breaks down and a spark jumps across. **Lightning** shows that at very high voltage even air can become conductive. Dry air can withstand about 3,000 volts per millimetre before it breaks down. In thunderstorms, voltages of many millions of volts build up between clouds and the ground.

Insulation protects people from dangerous **electric shocks**. That is why you must never touch damaged cables with visible wires and should replace them immediately. With overhead lines the rule is: never climb pylons and never fly kites near power lines, because electricity can also jump across through the air. The word insulator is also used for materials that conduct heat poorly, such as polystyrene or glass wool. Many good electrical insulators are also good heat insulators.

begriffe.erklaerung: A material through which electric current can flow well, for example copper.
A tiny, negatively charged particle that carries the current in metals.
The force that drives the current, measured in volts.
How high a voltage an insulating material can withstand before a spark breaks through.

gewusst: Birds can sit on a high-voltage line because they touch only one cable and no current flows through them.
Completely pure water conducts electricity very poorly; only dissolved salts make it conductive.
The insulator chains of large high-voltage lines can be several metres long.

teile.einleitung: High-voltage direct current transmission, HVDC for short, is a technique for transporting very large amounts of electrical energy over long distances. Instead of alternating current, direct current at a very high voltage flows through the line. It is especially important for long submarine cables and for wind power produced far away from where it is used.
wichtigste: HVDC transports electricity as direct current at a very high voltage.
Over very long distances the losses are lower than with alternating current, and there is no reactive power.
Converter stations convert alternating current into direct current and back again.
The expensive converter installations at both ends are the biggest cost disadvantage.
HVDC can connect power grids that are not synchronised.
The first commercial HVDC link went into operation in 1954 between the Swedish mainland and Gotland.
Since 2021 the NordLink submarine cable has connected Germany and Norway.

abschnitte.text: In our power grids, **alternating current** usually flows; in Europe it changes direction 50 times per second. With HVDC the electricity is converted into **direct current** for transport, which always flows in the same direction. The voltage is often several hundred thousand volts. At the destination the electricity is converted back into alternating current.

The conversion takes place in large **converter stations**, which can be as big as factory halls. Older installations work with semiconductor components called thyristors. Modern voltage source converters, VSC for short, use **IGBTs**, which can switch very quickly. These installations are expensive, which is why HVDC is worthwhile mainly over long distances.

With alternating current, long lines and especially cables produce **reactive power**, which also flows back and forth and puts a load on the line. With direct current there is none, and transmission losses are lower. That is why long submarine cables with alternating current work only over short distances. In addition, HVDC can connect two power grids that do not run in step.

In 1954 the first commercial HVDC link went into operation between the Swedish mainland and the island of **Gotland**. Since 2021 the **NordLink** submarine cable has connected Germany with Norway so that wind power and hydropower can be exchanged. In Germany the SuedLink project is meant to bring wind power from the north to the south with underground cables. In China there are HVDC lines more than 3,000 kilometres long.

Switzerland lies in the middle of the European interconnected grid, which runs on alternating current in step. But HVDC technology is also developed by companies closely connected with Switzerland. Part of it comes from the history of ABB, which was formed in 1988 from the Swedish company ASEA and the Swiss company Brown, Boveri & Cie. in Baden. ASEA had already built the Gotland link.

begriffe.erklaerung: Current that always flows in the same direction, as from a battery.
Current that keeps changing direction, as from a socket.
Installation that converts alternating current into direct current or the other way round.
Current that swings back and forth in lines and does no useful work.
A semiconductor switch that can switch large currents on and off very quickly.

gewusst: In the 19th century Thomas Edison and supporters of alternating current argued about which kind of current should win.
An HVDC line needs fewer conductors than an alternating current line and can therefore be built narrower.
With HVDC cables on the sea floor, wind farms far out at sea can be connected.

teile.einleitung: A helicopter is an aircraft with large rotating rotor blades on its roof. It can take off and land vertically and even stay still in the air. That is why it is ideal for rescues and transport in the mountains.
wichtigste: In Switzerland the word usually used is “Helikopter” rather than “Hubschrauber”.
The large main rotor creates lift and raises the helicopter into the air.
The small tail rotor stops the helicopter from turning in circles.
A helicopter can stay still in the air and needs no long runway.
In 1939 Igor Sikorsky built one of the first really usable helicopters.
In Switzerland you reach the air rescue service Rega on 1414.
Landing pads for helicopters are often marked with a large H.

abschnitte.text: The long **rotor blades** on the roof are curved like small wings. When they turn fast, they create **lift** and raise the helicopter. The pilot can change the angle of the blades. In this way the helicopter climbs, descends or flies forwards, backwards and sideways. It can even stay still in one place in the air.

abschnitte.titel: What is the small rotor at the back for?
abschnitte.text: When the big rotor turns in one direction, the body tries to turn in the other direction. The small **tail rotor** on the tail prevents this. It pushes the tail sideways and keeps the helicopter straight. Some helicopters instead have two main rotors that turn in opposite directions. Others use an enclosed tail rotor, which you can recognise by the round opening in the tail.

Around 1490 **Leonardo da Vinci** already drew a screw-shaped flying machine. But helicopters could only really fly in the 20th century. In Germany the Focke-Wulf Fw 61 flew in 1936. In 1939 the engineer **Igor Sikorsky** built one of the first really usable helicopters in the USA. After that, helicopters were quickly used for rescues, transport and the military.

In Switzerland helicopters are essential in the mountains. They bring **supplies and building materials** to mountain huts that no road reaches. They carry parts for cable cars and avalanche barriers. Mountain farmers sometimes have materials brought by helicopter too. Because helicopters need no long runway, they can land almost anywhere there is enough room for the rotor blades.

The Swiss air rescue service **Rega** was founded in 1952 and can be reached on **1414**. Its helicopters rescue injured people in the mountains, after accidents or in emergencies in remote places. With a **winch**, rescuers can also lift people off steep rock faces. Many hospitals have a landing pad on the roof. It is usually marked with a large H, which stands for helicopter.

begriffe.erklaerung: The turning blades that lift the helicopter into the air.
The small rotor at the back that stops the body from turning.
A force that acts upwards and carries the aircraft.
The Swiss air rescue service, emergency number 1414.
A device used to pull people up on a cable.

gewusst: A helicopter can fly backwards and sideways; an aeroplane cannot.
The word helicopter comes from Greek and means roughly “spiral wing”.
Rega is largely financed by patrons from the general public.

teile.einleitung: An integrated circuit, IC for short or simply a chip, is a whole electronic circuit on a tiny wafer of semiconductor material. Billions of transistors can fit on it. Today chips are found in almost every device, from mobile phones to washing machines.
wichtigste: An integrated circuit combines many electronic components on a single chip.
The first integrated circuit was made in 1958 and was made of germanium.
In 1959 the Geneva-born physicist Jean Hoerni invented the planar process.
Today chips are usually made of silicon on wafers 300 millimetres across.
A single chip piece sawn out of the wafer is called a die.
Special-purpose chips are called ASICs, freely configurable chips FPGAs.
A system on a chip combines almost a whole computer on one chip.

abschnitte.text: In the past, electronic circuits were built from many individual components connected by wires. In an **integrated circuit**, transistors, resistors and conducting tracks are all combined on a small **semiconductor wafer**. This saves an enormous amount of space and electricity. The circuits also become more reliable and cheaper. Almost all modern electronic devices are based on such chips.

In 1958 **Jack Kilby** at Texas Instruments built the first integrated circuit, made of germanium. Shortly afterwards **Robert Noyce** at Fairchild developed a chip made of silicon. This was made possible by the **planar process**, which the Geneva-born physicist Jean Hoerni invented in 1959. With it, flat, protected structures could be made on silicon. Jack Kilby received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2000.

Chips are made on **wafers**, thin silicon discs up to 300 millimetres across. In many steps, extremely fine structures are applied using photolithography, etching and coating. In this way hundreds of chips are made on one wafer at the same time. Then the wafer is sawn up; each individual piece is called a **die**. It is fitted into a package, for example a DIP with two rows of connecting legs.

An **ASIC** is a chip designed specially for a single task. An **FPGA**, on the other hand, can be programmed by the user after it has been made. A system on a chip combines a processor, graphics, memory control and more, as in mobile phones. There are also memory chips, sensor chips and many others. Chips with millions to billions of transistors are also called VLSI, for very large scale integration.

In 1965 Gordon Moore predicted that the number of transistors on a chip would double regularly. This **Moore's law** held for a surprisingly long time. Early chips had only a few transistors; today's top chips have many billions. That is why computers today are much more powerful and at the same time smaller than in the past. Chips have become so important that countries compete to make them.

begriffe.erklaerung: A material such as silicon that conducts electricity only under certain conditions.
A tiny electronic switch.
A thin silicon disc on which many chips are made.
A single chip piece sawn out of the wafer.
A chip built specially for a single application.

gewusst: Jack Kilby's first integrated circuit had only one transistor and was still connected with small wires.
The inventor of the planar process, Jean Hoerni, came from Geneva.
A modern car often contains more than a thousand chips.

teile.einleitung: Guglielmo Marconi was an Italian inventor and businessman who made wireless telegraphy by radio known all over the world. In 1901 he achieved the first radio transmission across the Atlantic. Without his work there might be no radio, no ship radio and no mobile phones today.
wichtigste: Marconi was born in Bologna in Italy in 1874 and died in Rome in 1937.
He is known above all for wireless telegraphy by radio.
In 1896 he moved to Great Britain because he found support for his experiments there.
In 1901 he sent the Morse letter S across the Atlantic without wires.
In 1909 he received the Nobel Prize in Physics together with Ferdinand Braun.
When the Titanic sank in 1912, radio operators called for help with Marconi equipment.

abschnitte.text: Guglielmo Marconi was born on 25 April 1874 in **Bologna**. His father was an Italian landowner and his mother came from Ireland. Even as a teenager he was very interested in electricity and read everything about the **electromagnetic waves** that Heinrich Hertz had discovered. Around 1895 he began his own experiments on his family's estate near Bologna.

Marconi built a transmitter and a receiver and set them up further and further apart. With a high **aerial** and a connection to the earth, the range became much greater. Soon he could send signals over a hill, with no line of sight. But in Italy he found hardly any interest in his invention.

abschnitte.titel: A new start in Great Britain
abschnitte.text: In 1896 Marconi moved to **Great Britain**, where the British Post Office supported his experiments. There he applied for a patent and in 1897 founded his own radio company. In 1899 he achieved a radio link across the English Channel to France. His equipment was quickly fitted on ships, because a wireless connection was especially valuable there.

On 12 December 1901 Marconi attempted his biggest experiment: a transmitter at Poldhu in Cornwall (England) sent signals across the **Atlantic**. Marconi waited in Newfoundland in Canada and held the aerial up in the air with a kite. He heard the Morse letter **S**, that is, three short tones. Many experts had not believed that radio waves could follow the curve of the Earth.

In 1909 Marconi received the Nobel Prize in Physics together with the German physicist **Ferdinand Braun**. When the **Titanic** sank in April 1912, the radio operators on board sent distress calls with Marconi equipment. The ship Carpathia received the calls and rescued over 700 people. After that, radio became compulsory on large ships everywhere.

Marconi's radio telegraphy later developed into **radio** broadcasting, aircraft radio and mobile phones. That is why Marconi is considered one of the most important pioneers of radio technology. He died in Rome on 20 July 1937. Today streets, schools and an airport in Bologna bear his name.

begriffe.erklaerung: Sending messages over long distances, for example with Morse code.
Transmitting signals without cables using electromagnetic waves.
A code of short and long signals with which letters can be transmitted.
A metal rod or wire that sends out or receives radio waves.

gewusst: In Marconi's Atlantic experiment, the receiving aerial hung from a kite because the wind had torn away a balloon.
When Marconi died in 1937, many radio transmitters around the world fell silent for two minutes in his honour.
Marconi was only 35 years old when he received the Nobel Prize.

teile.einleitung: The motherboard is the large circuit board inside a computer on which all the important components sit. In German it is called the “Hauptplatine” (main board). It connects the processor, working memory, graphics card and all the other parts with each other.
wichtigste: The motherboard is also often called the mainboard.
Its main job is to connect all the components of the computer with each other.
The processor sits in a holder called a socket.
Fine copper tracks carry electricity and signals.
A button cell battery keeps the time and basic settings when the computer is switched off.
The start-up software BIOS or UEFI is stored on the motherboard.
Graphics cards are usually plugged into a PCI Express slot today.
ATX is a widespread standard format for motherboards in desktop computers.

abschnitte.text: The motherboard is a flat board made of plastic and glass fibre on which many electronic parts are mounted. You can compare it with the **nervous system** of a computer. All the components exchange their data through it. Without a motherboard, no part can work together with any other.

In the middle sits the **socket** for the processor, the computer's calculating centre. Next to it are slots for the **working memory**, into which long memory sticks are plugged. For graphics cards there are slots following the **PCI Express** standard. On top of this come connections for hard disks, fast M.2 storage and for USB, network and sound.

The fine lines on the board are copper **tracks**. They work like tiny roads for electricity and data. Often they lie in several layers on top of each other so that there is enough room. A special chip, the **chipset**, controls the traffic between the processor and the other connections.

A small memory chip holds the start-up software **BIOS** or its modern successor **UEFI**. When the computer is switched on, it checks the components and then starts the operating system. A small round button cell battery supplies the built-in clock with power. This means the computer still knows the time and date after being switched off.

So that motherboards fit into every case, there are fixed sizes. The best-known format for desktop computers is **ATX**, which the company Intel introduced in 1995. Smaller formats are called, for example, Micro-ATX and Mini-ITX. Laptops, tablets and mobile phones also have motherboards, but they are much smaller and tailored exactly to the device.

begriffe.erklaerung: The main circuit board of a computer, “Hauptplatine” in German.
The chip that does the calculating work in the computer.
Holder on the motherboard into which the processor is fitted.
Chip that controls the data traffic on the motherboard.
Modern start-up software that prepares the computer when it is switched on.

gewusst: A motherboard can consist of many layers of tracks on top of each other, even though it is only a few millimetres thick.
The button cell on the motherboard often lasts many years before it needs changing.
There is a motherboard inside a games console too.

teile.einleitung: Hedy Lamarr was an Austrian-American film actress and inventor. She became world-famous as a film star in Hollywood, but on the side she tinkered with technical ideas. Together with the composer George Antheil she invented frequency hopping, whose principle is found today, for example, in Bluetooth.
wichtigste: Hedy Lamarr was born in Vienna on 9 November 1914 and died in the USA in 2000.
At first she was world-famous as a film actress in Hollywood.
With the composer George Antheil she developed frequency hopping.
The invention was meant to steer torpedoes by radio without interference.
Transmitter and receiver were to change frequency at the same time using identically punched paper rolls.
Today's radio technologies such as Bluetooth use the principle of changing frequency.
On her birthday Germany, Austria and Switzerland celebrate Inventors' Day.

abschnitte.text: Hedy Lamarr's real name was **Hedwig Kiesler**, and she grew up in **Vienna**. As a young woman she already acted in films in Austria and Germany. In 1937 she went to the USA, where a big film studio signed her up and gave her the name Hedy Lamarr. She acted in many Hollywood films and was considered one of the best-known actresses of her time.

As well as filming, Hedy Lamarr was very interested in technology. At home she had a workbench where she worked on ideas. During the **Second World War** she wanted to help the opponents of Nazi Germany. She thought about how remote-controlled torpedoes could be protected from interference.

A radio signal on just one frequency is easy for an enemy to find and jam. Lamarr's idea: transmitter and receiver keep changing **frequency** in the same rhythm. Anyone who does not know the sequence hears only fragments. This is how **frequency hopping** came about.

Her partner was the American composer **George Antheil**, who had written music for mechanical pianos. He suggested controlling the frequency changes with **punched paper rolls**, similar to a self-playing piano. Their system had 88 frequencies, as many as a piano has keys. In 1942 the two received a patent for it in the USA.

The American navy did not use the invention at the time. Only decades later did the principle become important in radio technology. Today **Bluetooth** and other radio methods use rapid frequency changes so that connections are stable and hard to disturb. Hedy Lamarr only received awards for her invention towards the end of her life, and since 2014 her name has been in the American National Inventors Hall of Fame.

begriffe.erklaerung: How often a wave oscillates per second; in radio, something like a channel.
Radio technique in which transmitter and receiver keep changing frequency together.
A right that protects an invention for a certain time.
Strip of paper with holes that a machine reads like a program.

gewusst: The 88 frequencies in Lamarr's patent correspond exactly to the number of keys on a piano.
Inventors' Day on 9 November was chosen because it is Hedy Lamarr's birthday.
Hedy Lamarr never sold her invention and earned no money from it.

teile.einleitung: A hybrid drive combines two different kinds of drive in one vehicle, usually a combustion engine and an electric motor. In this way a car can save fuel, because the electric motor helps when pulling away and braking energy is recovered. The word hybrid means something like mixed or crossed.
wichtigste: A hybrid drive usually combines a combustion engine with an electric motor.
In a series hybrid, the combustion engine only drives a generator.
The battery of a plug-in hybrid can be charged from the mains.
A mild hybrid with a 48-volt system usually cannot drive longer distances on electricity alone.
The Toyota Prius came onto the market in Japan in 1997 as the first mass-produced hybrid car.
Around 1900 Ferdinand Porsche built one of the first hybrid cars, the Semper Vivus.
In town traffic with frequent pulling away and braking, a full hybrid saves especially a lot of fuel.

abschnitte.text: A hybrid car has two hearts: a petrol or diesel engine and an **electric motor** with a battery. The computer in the car constantly decides which motor is working at the moment or whether both drive together. When braking, the electric motor works as a generator and charges the battery. This recovery of braking energy is called **regenerative braking**.

In a **series hybrid**, the combustion engine only drives a generator, and only the electric motor moves the wheels. In a parallel hybrid, both motors can act directly on the wheels. In a power-split hybrid, a **planetary gear** divides the engine's power between the wheels and the generator. Toyota, for example, uses this solution.

A **mild hybrid** usually has a 48-volt system and supports the engine only a little; it cannot manage longer distances on electricity alone. A full hybrid can drive short distances slowly on electricity only. In a **plug-in hybrid** the battery is bigger and can be charged at a socket or charging station. This often makes a few dozen kilometres possible on electricity alone.

A combustion engine works poorly when pulling away and at low load. That is exactly where the electric motor helps, which is why a full hybrid saves fuel above all in **town traffic** with many traffic lights. Many full hybrids use petrol engines based on the Atkinson or Miller principle, which are more economical thanks to a longer expansion of the gases. On the motorway at a steady speed, on the other hand, the advantage is smaller.

As early as around 1900, **Ferdinand Porsche** built one of the first hybrid cars, the Lohner-Porsche Semper Vivus. After that, pure petrol and diesel cars won out for a long time. In 1997 the **Toyota Prius** came onto the market in Japan, the first hybrid car to be built in large numbers. Today many buses, ships and even Formula 1 racing cars also run with hybrid drive.

begriffe.erklaerung: Recovering energy when braking in order to charge the battery.
Machine that converts movement into electric current.
The car can be plugged in and charged at a socket.
Gear with gearwheels that circle around a central wheel like planets.

gewusst: Semper Vivus is Latin and means always alive.
Many hybrid cars drive completely silently in car parks, because only the electric motor is running.
Diesel-electric locomotives work in a similar way to a series hybrid.

teile.einleitung: Johannes Gutenberg was an inventor from Mainz who invented printing with movable metal letters in the 15th century. Suddenly books could be produced quickly and in large numbers, instead of every word being copied by hand. Many people consider his invention one of the most important in human history.
wichtigste: Johannes Gutenberg lived in the 15th century; he was born around 1400 and died in 1468.
He lived and printed in Mainz, which is in Germany today.
He invented printing with movable metal type.
His most famous work is the Gutenberg Bible.
About 180 Gutenberg Bibles were printed.
Besides books, he also printed letters of indulgence.
In Mainz the Gutenberg Museum remembers him.

abschnitte.text: Johannes Gutenberg's real name was Johannes Gensfleisch, and he was born around 1400 in **Mainz** on the Rhine. He took the name Gutenberg from a house belonging to his family, the “Hof zum Gutenberg”. He lived for some years in **Strasbourg**, where he worked with metal and probably already made his first printing experiments. Later he returned to Mainz, where he died in 1468.

Gutenberg's big idea was **movable type**: individual letters made of metal that could be put together into words and pages and then used again. With a **hand mould** he cast thousands of letters of the same size from a mixture of lead, tin and antimony. A **printing press**, similar to a wine press, pressed the paper onto the inked letters. For this he mixed a special oil-based printing ink that stuck well to the metal.

Around 1452 to 1454 Gutenberg printed the Latin Bible, now called the **Gutenberg Bible**. Each page has two columns, usually with 42 lines, and it runs to about 1,280 pages. About 180 copies were printed, most on paper, some on expensive parchment. Today about 49 of them still exist, and they are among the most valuable books in the world.

For his workshop Gutenberg needed a lot of money and borrowed it from the merchant **Johannes Fust**. In 1455 Fust demanded the money back, and after a legal dispute Gutenberg lost part of his workshop. With smaller jobs such as **letters of indulgence**, calendars and school books he earned extra money. Later he received a kind of honorary pension from the Archbishop of Mainz.

Within a few decades, print shops appeared all over Europe, including in **Basel**, which soon became an important printing city. Books became cheaper, more people learnt to read, and knowledge spread much faster. Without printing, the ideas of the **Reformation** would hardly have spread so quickly either. In Mainz the **Gutenberg Museum** remembers the inventor and shows original Bibles.

begriffe.erklaerung: Individual metal letters for printing.
Machine that presses paper firmly onto the inked type.
Expensive writing material made from treated animal skin.
Church document in the Middle Ages that could be obtained for money.
Church reform movement in the 16th century from which the Reformed churches arose.

gewusst: Nobody knows exactly what Gutenberg looked like, because there is no picture painted during his lifetime.
Before printing existed, monks often spent months or years copying a thick book by hand.
Gutenberg's Bible contains neither his name nor a printing date.

teile.einleitung: A hot-air balloon is an aircraft that flies without wings or an engine. It rises because the heated air in its huge envelope is lighter than the cool air outside. Balloon flights are one of the oldest ways in which people have got into the air.
wichtigste: The air in the balloon envelope is heated with a gas burner.
The passengers stand in a basket under the envelope.
The Montgolfier brothers built the first hot-air balloons in France.
In 1783 a sheep, a duck and a cockerel flew along as the first passengers.
In German, balloonists say “fahren” (to travel) instead of “fliegen” (to fly).
The direction is chosen by looking for winds at other heights.
Every winter a big balloon festival takes place in the mountain village of Château-d'Oex in Vaud.

abschnitte.text: Warm air expands and is therefore lighter than cold air. If the air in the **envelope** is much warmer than the surrounding air, **lift** is created that carries the balloon, basket and people upwards. If the pilot wants to climb, he heats more with the burner. If the air cools down, or he lets warm air escape through an opening at the top, the balloon sinks.

The envelope is made of light, tear-resistant fabric such as nylon or polyester and is often as tall as a house with several storeys. Below it hangs the **gas burner**, which burns propane from cylinders and produces loud, hot flames. The passengers stand in a **basket** made of woven willow or rattan. This material is light and stable and cushions the landing.

In 1783 the French brothers Joseph-Michel and Jacques-Étienne **Montgolfier** launched the first hot-air balloons. In September 1783, at Versailles in front of the king, a sheep, a duck and a cockerel went up and landed unhurt. In November 1783 people travelled in a hot-air balloon for the first time, in Paris. That is why a hot-air balloon is also called a **montgolfière**.

A balloon has no steering and drifts with the wind. Because the wind often blows from different directions at different heights, the pilot climbs or descends to find a suitable air current. Balloons usually take off early in the morning or in the evening, when the air is calm. A chase vehicle follows on the ground to collect the balloon and passengers after landing.

Every winter an international balloon festival takes place in the mountain village of **Château-d'Oex** in Vaud, where many colourful balloons travel over the snowy Alps. In 1999 the balloon Breitling Orbiter 3 also set off from there with the Swiss **Bertrand Piccard** and the Briton Brian Jones. They were the first to travel all the way round the Earth in a balloon without landing. Their balloon, however, was a mixture of a gas balloon and a hot-air balloon.

begriffe.erklaerung: Force that pushes something lighter upwards in air or water.
The big fabric bag of the balloon, which is filled with hot air.
Another name for a hot-air balloon, after the Montgolfier brothers.
A gas carried in cylinders and burned in the burner.

gewusst: In German, balloonists say “fahren” instead of “fliegen”, because the balloon drifts with the flow of the air like a ship.
The first passengers of a balloon were not people but a sheep, a duck and a cockerel.
In the basket you feel almost no wind, because the balloon drifts exactly as fast as the air around it.

teile.einleitung: The internet is a worldwide network that connects billions of computers, mobile phones and other devices with each other. Over the internet we send messages, watch videos, look for information and play together. An important part of it, the World Wide Web, was invented in Switzerland at CERN near Geneva.
wichtigste: The internet connects devices all over the world with each other.
Its forerunner is considered to be ARPANET, which was set up in the USA from 1969.
In 1989 Tim Berners-Lee invented the World Wide Web at CERN near Geneva.
With a browser you call up and look at web pages.
An IP address is a number that identifies a device on the network.
The “s” in “https” stands for secure.
Swiss internet addresses often end in .ch.

abschnitte.text: The internet consists of many networks connected by cable, radio and satellite. Each device has an **IP address**, a number that identifies it on the network, rather like a postal address. Data is split into small packets and sent separately. At the destination they are put back together. So that all devices understand each other, shared rules apply, the **protocols**, for example TCP/IP.

From 1969 **ARPANET** was set up in the USA; it is considered the forerunner of the internet. At first it connected only a few universities. In 1989 **Tim Berners-Lee** at CERN near Geneva proposed the World Wide Web, a system of linked pages. In 1991 the first website went online. From the mid-1990s the internet spread into many households.

The **World Wide Web** is the part of the internet with web pages connected by links. With a **browser** such as Firefox, Chrome or Safari you call up web pages. Every page has an address, the URL. If it begins with “https”, the data is transmitted encrypted; the “s” stands for secure. Search engines help you find the right page among billions.

Swiss internet addresses have the **country code** .ch, which comes from the Latin name Confoederatio Helvetica. The endings .ch and .li are allocated by the SWITCH foundation. Almost all households in Switzerland have internet today, many with fast fibre-optic lines. At **CERN**, research is still carried out at the forefront of science, and the first website can be viewed online there again.

On the internet you should not give personal data such as your address or passwords to strangers. A good **password** is long and is not used for several services. Not everything on the internet is true, so it is worth checking sources. Anyone who is treated nastily should turn to their parents or teachers. Shared rules for screen time help you use the internet sensibly.

begriffe.erklaerung: Number that identifies a device on the internet.
Program for looking at web pages.
Rules that let computers exchange data.
Connection that takes you to another page with a click.
Converting data so that only the recipient can read it.

gewusst: The world's very first website ran on a computer at CERN with a note stuck on it saying it must not be switched off.
Under the oceans lie hundreds of submarine cables that carry most of the world's internet traffic.
In 1993 CERN released the World Wide Web so that everyone could use it free of charge.

teile.einleitung: Semiconductors are materials that conduct electricity better than insulators such as glass, but worse than metals such as copper. Their conductivity can be controlled deliberately, and that is exactly what makes them so valuable. Without semiconductors there would be no computers, smartphones, LED lamps or solar cells.
wichtigste: Semiconductors conduct electricity better than insulators, but worse than metals.
Silicon is the most important basic material of the semiconductor industry.
Doping with foreign atoms such as phosphorus changes the conductivity.
As the temperature rises, a pure semiconductor conducts better.
A diode consists of a p-n junction and lets current through in only one direction.
In 1947 the first working transistor was demonstrated at Bell Labs.
In 1958 Jack Kilby built the first integrated circuit at Texas Instruments.

abschnitte.text: In metals many electrons can move freely, which is why they conduct electricity well. In insulators the electrons are tightly bound. In **semiconductors** an electron needs a small boost of energy to break free. This energy is called the **band gap**; for silicon at room temperature it is about 1.1 electronvolts. When a pure semiconductor gets warmer, more electrons are freed and it conducts better, unlike a metal.

Pure **silicon** conducts only a little. That is why tiny amounts of foreign atoms are mixed in; this is called **doping**. With phosphorus, extra free electrons are created; this is called n-doping. With boron, gaps called holes are created; this is p-doping. Where an n region and a p region meet, a **p-n junction** forms.

A **diode** consists of a p-n junction and lets current through in only one direction, like a valve. Light-emitting diodes, that is LEDs, give off light as they do so. A **transistor** can switch current on and off or amplify it; it is the basic building block of every computer. The first working transistor was demonstrated in 1947 at Bell Labs in the USA. John Bardeen, Walter Brattain and William Shockley received the Nobel Prize in Physics for it in 1956.

In 1958 Jack Kilby built the first **integrated circuit** at Texas Instruments, in which several components sit on a single piece of semiconductor. Today modern chips contain billions of transistors. They are made on thin silicon discs, the **wafers**. The most modern chips are made with EUV lithography, which uses light with a wavelength of 13.5 nanometres. The machines for this are built by the Dutch company ASML.

Semiconductors are found in mobile phones, cars, washing machines and **solar cells**. Silicon is obtained from quartz sand, one of the most common substances on Earth. Many of the most modern chips are made in Taiwan. In Switzerland, the semiconductor maker STMicroelectronics has its headquarters near Geneva. Because chips are so important, some people call silicon the “raw material of the digital age”.

begriffe.erklaerung: Energy an electron needs to move freely in a semiconductor.
Deliberately adding foreign atoms to change the conductivity.
Tiny electronic switch and amplifier.
Thin disc of silicon on which chips are made.
Component that lets current through in only one direction.

gewusst: Silicon Valley in California is named after silicon.
Chip factories must be much cleaner than an operating theatre, because even tiny specks of dust destroy a chip.
A single modern smartphone chip contains more transistors than there are people on Earth.

teile.einleitung: James Watt was a Scottish inventor and engineer who made decisive improvements to the steam engine. His engines drove the Industrial Revolution. The unit of power, the watt, is named after him.
wichtigste: James Watt came from Scotland and lived from 1736 to 1819.
He improved the older steam engine of Thomas Newcomen.
With the businessman Matthew Boulton he built steam engines in large numbers in Birmingham.
The first Boulton & Watt engines mainly pumped water out of mines.
In his double-acting steam engine, the steam pushes the piston alternately from both sides.
To compare engines, he used horsepower.
The unit of power, the watt, bears his name.

abschnitte.text: James Watt was born in 1736 in **Greenock** in Scotland. He learnt the trade of instrument maker. At the University of Glasgow he repaired scientific equipment. One day he was given a model of **Thomas Newcomen's** steam engine to repair. In doing so he noticed how much energy this engine wasted.

In Newcomen's engine, the cylinder was cooled and heated again with every stroke. This cost a great deal of coal. Watt had the idea of a **separate condenser**, in which the steam is cooled while the cylinder stays hot. In 1769 he patented his invention. His engine needed only about a quarter of the coal that Newcomen's engine used.

From 1775 Watt worked with the businessman **Matthew Boulton** in Birmingham. Their company, Boulton & Watt, built steam engines in large numbers. At first these mainly pumped **water out of mines**. Later Watt developed the double-acting steam engine, in which the steam pushes the piston alternately from both sides. With a rotary motion, the engines could now also drive spinning mills and other mills.

To show customers how powerful his engines were, Watt compared them with horses. This gave rise to the unit **horsepower**, hp for short. After his death he was honoured with a unit of his own. The **watt** is today the unit of power, for example for light bulbs, hairdryers or power stations. From 2011 Boulton and Watt also appeared on the British 50-pound note.

Watt had many talents. In 1780 he invented a **copying press** to duplicate letters. He also improved measuring instruments and worked on chemistry. His steam engines drove the **Industrial Revolution** and changed work and life throughout Europe. James Watt died in 1819 near Birmingham.

begriffe.erklaerung: A machine that works with the power of hot steam.
Here, a container in which steam is cooled and turns back into water.
A movable cylinder that is pushed back and forth by steam pressure.
An old unit for the power of engines, hp for short.
Today's unit of power.

gewusst: Watt is said to have had the idea of the separate condenser while out on a Sunday walk.
One metric horsepower equals about 735 watts.
Watt received a patent for his steam engine that lasted so long that other inventors could hardly compete for decades.

teile.einleitung: The central processing unit, CPU for short, is the calculating centre of a computer. It carries out the instructions of all programs, from games to word processing. It is often called the “brain” of the computer.
wichtigste: CPU stands for central processing unit, “Hauptprozessor” in German.
The processor carries out the instructions of the programs.
Billions of tiny switches, the transistors, work in a modern processor.
The clock speed is given in gigahertz.
A quad-core processor has four processing units that can work at the same time.
The cache is a very fast buffer memory directly inside the processor.
Processors are made mainly of silicon and need cooling.

abschnitte.text: Every program consists of many simple **instructions**, for example “add two numbers” or “store this value”. The central processor fetches these instructions from the working memory and carries them out one after another. This happens incredibly fast, billions of times per second. The processor works closely with the **working memory** and the graphics card. Without a processor, a computer could do nothing at all.

A processor works in a fixed rhythm, the **clock**. The clock speed is measured in gigahertz; one gigahertz means a billion clock cycles per second. Modern processors have several **cores**, that is, several processing units on one chip. A quad-core processor can work on four tasks at the same time. This helps, for example, when you listen to music, surf the web and load a game at the same time.

A processor is a **computer chip** made of silicon. On it there are billions of tiny electronic switches, the **transistors**. They can only have two states, on or off, that is, one or zero. From many such switches, arithmetic units, control units and memory are built. The **cache** is an especially fast buffer memory directly inside the processor, where frequently used data is kept ready.

When calculating, a processor produces a lot of **heat**. That is why there is usually a metal heat sink with a fan on top of it. Thermal paste goes between the processor and the cooler so that the heat can flow away well. If a processor gets too hot, it slows itself down to avoid damage. Mobile phones have no fan; their processors are built to be especially economical.

In 1971 the company Intel brought out the **Intel 4004**, one of the first microprocessors. It had only about 2,300 transistors; today's processors have billions. Most processors for Windows PCs come from **Intel** and **AMD**. Mobile phones and many Apple computers contain processors with the economical ARM design. Today small processors also work in cars, washing machines and coffee machines.

begriffe.erklaerung: Abbreviation for central processing unit.
A tiny electronic switch.
How many working steps per second the processor manages.
A processing unit in the processor that can work independently.
A very fast buffer memory in the processor.

gewusst: The transistors in modern processors are so small that thousands would fit side by side across the thickness of a hair.
The first microprocessor of 1971 was originally intended for a desktop calculator from Japan.
A mobile phone today has more computing power than the computers used to control the Moon landing in 1969.

teile.einleitung: The Grande Dixence is a huge dam in the canton of Valais and, at 285 metres, the highest gravity dam in the world. Behind it lies the reservoir Lac des Dix, whose water produces electricity in power stations. The installation is one of the most important hydropower plants in Switzerland.
wichtigste: The Grande Dixence stands in the canton of Valais at the end of the Val des Dix.
Behind the dam lies the reservoir Lac des Dix.
The highest water level is at about 2,360 metres above sea level.
The dam is made of concrete and is 285 metres high.
As a gravity dam, it holds back the water by its own enormous weight.
Part of the water is pumped here from valleys as far away as near Zermatt.
In 2019 the Bieudron power station produced more electricity than any other Swiss hydropower station.

abschnitte.text: The Grande Dixence lies high up in the **Val des Dix**, a side valley of the Val d'Hérens in the canton of **Valais**. It is not far to the next larger valley and to Sion, but all around there are glaciers and peaks over 3,000 metres. Behind the dam stretches the reservoir **Lac des Dix**, whose water level when the lake is full is at about 2,360 metres above sea level. In summer you can take a small cable car up to the top of the dam and walk along the lake.

The dam was built in the 1950s and completed in 1961. It is 285 metres high, almost as high as the Eiffel Tower, and consists of about 6 million cubic metres of **concrete**. As a **gravity dam**, it holds back the water pressure purely by its enormous weight, which is why it is very wide at the bottom. Inside there are passages in which experts regularly check the dam.

The reservoir holds about 400 million cubic metres of water. It comes mainly from the **meltwater** of glaciers, which flows plentifully in summer. Because its own valley does not supply enough, tunnels collect water from neighbouring valleys. With **pumping stations**, water is even carried up from the area near Zermatt and through the mountains to the Lac des Dix.

In winter, when a lot of electricity is needed, the water flows down through steep **penstocks** into the Rhône valley. There it drives turbines in power stations such as Fionnay, Nendaz and **Bieudron**, which turn generators. Bieudron uses a head of almost 1,900 metres, which was a world record when it opened in 1998. After an accident in 2000 it stood still for about ten years, but in 2019 it produced more electricity than any other Swiss hydropower station.

In Switzerland hydropower supplies about half to almost two thirds of the electricity. Storage lakes such as the Lac des Dix are especially valuable because they collect water in summer and supply the electricity only in winter. That is why they are also called the **batteries of the Alps**. Because of **glacier retreat**, the amount of meltwater the installations receive will change in future.

begriffe.erklaerung: Wall that blocks a valley and holds water back to form a lake.
Dam that holds back the water purely by its weight.
Reservoir that collects water to produce electricity later.
Thick pipe in which water flows steeply down to the turbines.
Wheel that is turned by water and drives a generator.

gewusst: More concrete went into the Grande Dixence than stone into the Pyramid of Cheops.
During construction, over a thousand workers lived in their own settlement high up in the valley.
In spring the Lac des Dix is often almost empty and only fills with glacier water in summer.

teile.einleitung: ITER is a huge experimental reactor meant to show that energy can be obtained from nuclear fusion. In it, atomic nuclei are to fuse together, as happens in the sun. It is being built in Cadarache in southern France by several countries together.
wichtigste: ITER is an international experimental reactor for nuclear fusion.
It is being built in Cadarache in southern France.
Seven equal partners are involved, including the EU, China, India, Japan, South Korea, Russia and the USA.
The ITER agreement was signed in Paris in 2006.
ITER is meant to produce ten times more fusion power than is put in for heating.
The Latin word “iter” means “the way”.
According to the 2024 schedule, experiments with deuterium and tritium are planned from 2039.

abschnitte.text: In the sun, light atomic nuclei fuse into heavier ones, releasing a lot of energy. This process is called **nuclear fusion**. ITER is meant to fuse nuclei of **deuterium** and **tritium**, two kinds of hydrogen. To do this they have to be heated to well over 100 million degrees, much hotter than inside the sun. At this heat the gas becomes a **plasma**.

No material can withstand such hot plasma. That is why in ITER it is held suspended by strong **magnetic fields**. The installation has the shape of a ring and is called a **tokamak**. The large toroidal field coils are made of the superconductor niobium tin and are cooled almost to absolute zero. The plasma is to have a volume of about 840 cubic metres.

ITER is meant, for the first time, to obtain more energy from fusion than is put in for heating. The goal is a **gain factor Q** of 10. This means that 50 megawatts of heating power should become 500 megawatts of fusion power. ITER is not yet meant to supply electricity to the grid. It is an experiment that should pave the way for later **fusion power stations**.

The agreement for ITER was signed in Paris in 2006. Seven partners work together as equals: the **European Union**, China, India, Japan, South Korea, Russia and the USA. The components are made in many countries and brought to southern France. Construction is taking much longer and costing much more than originally planned. According to the 2024 schedule, experiments with deuterium and tritium are to begin from 2039.

Deuterium can be obtained from ordinary seawater. Tritium hardly occurs in nature. In future fusion power stations, it is therefore to be bred from **lithium** in a layer around the plasma, the **blanket**. Fusion produces no CO2 and no long-lived radioactive waste like nuclear fission. In Switzerland, the Swiss Plasma Center of EPFL in Lausanne researches fusion with its own tokamak.

begriffe.erklaerung: The fusing of light atomic nuclei, which releases energy.
Extremely hot gas in which atoms break up into nuclei and electrons.
A ring-shaped installation that holds plasma in place with magnetic fields.
A material that, when cooled, conducts electricity without any resistance.
A special, heavy form of hydrogen.

gewusst: The plasma in ITER is to become about ten times hotter than the core of the sun.
Just a few metres away from the plasma at over 100 million degrees, the magnet coils are almost as cold as outer space.
A single gram of fusion fuel could supply as much energy as several tonnes of coal.

teile.einleitung: Information theory is a field of mathematics that studies how information can be measured, compressed and transmitted reliably. It was founded in 1948 by the American Claude Shannon. Without it, there would be no internet, no mobile phones and no streamed videos in their present form.
wichtigste: Claude Shannon founded information theory in 1948 with the paper A Mathematical Theory of Communication.
Information is measured in bits.
A fair coin toss has an entropy of 1 bit; a coin that always shows heads has 0 bits.
An event with a probability of 1/8 provides 3 bits of information.
For one of 26 equally likely characters you need about 4.7 bits.
Redundancy is the part of a message that is not needed for its content.
In channel coding, redundancy is added deliberately in order to detect and correct transmission errors.
The Shannon-Hartley formula C = B · log2(1 + S/N) gives the most a channel can transmit.

abschnitte.text: **Claude Shannon** (1916 to 2001) was an American mathematician and engineer. He worked at Bell Laboratories, the research laboratory of a large telephone company. In 1948 he published the paper A Mathematical Theory of Communication. In it he described exactly, for the first time, what information is mathematically.

The basic unit of information is the **bit**, the answer to a yes-or-no question. The less likely an event is, the more information it contains. An event with a probability of 1/8 provides 3 bits, because you need three yes-or-no questions to guess one of 8 results. A message that you already know for certain beforehand, on the other hand, contains no new information.

**Entropy** tells you how much information a source provides on average. A fair coin toss has exactly 1 bit; a coin with two heads has 0 bits, because the result is always clear. With 26 equally likely letters it is about 4.7 bits per character. In real texts, however, some letters such as E occur much more often, so the entropy is lower.

Many messages contain **redundancy**, that is, parts that are not needed for the content. That is why you can often still read a sentence when some letters are missing. In source coding, redundancy is removed so that files become smaller, as with ZIP files. Morse code already used this idea, because the frequent E consists of just a single short tone.

When transmitting by radio or cable, noise causes errors. That is why in **channel coding** redundancy is added deliberately, for example check digits. In this way the receiver can recognise errors and often even correct them. That is why a QR code can still be read when part of it is dirty.

Shannon showed that every transmission path has a highest possible data rate, the **channel capacity**. The Shannon-Hartley formula calculates it from the bandwidth and the ratio of signal to noise. So more bandwidth or a stronger signal allows more data per second. Engineers still use this limit today when building mobile networks, Wi-Fi and fibre-optic networks.

begriffe.erklaerung: Smallest unit of information, a yes-or-no answer or a 0 or 1.
Measure of how much information a source provides on average.
Part of a message that is not strictly needed for the content.
Random disturbances that distort a signal.
The largest amount of data a transmission path can manage per second.

gewusst: In his spare time Claude Shannon built a mechanical mouse that could learn its own way through a maze.
Because language has a lot of redundancy, you can often understand a text even when many letters are missing.
Every mobile phone call and every streaming video uses error correction based on the ideas of information theory.

teile.einleitung: A hammer is a tool used mainly for knocking in nails. It consists of a heavy head and a handle you hold it by. The hammer is one of the oldest tools of humankind.
wichtigste: A hammer is used mainly for knocking in nails.
A hammer consists of the hammer head and the handle.
With the split side of a claw hammer you can pull nails out.
The rubber mallet has a soft head so that nothing gets scratched.
A sledgehammer is so heavy that you swing it with both hands.
The blacksmith strikes glowing iron with a hammer on an anvil.
When hammering, safety glasses protect your eyes from splinters.

abschnitte.text: A hammer has a heavy **head** made of steel and a **handle**, usually made of wood such as ash or of plastic. The flat striking surface on the head is called the face. On the other side there is often a narrow edge, the peen, or a split claw. The head sits firmly on the handle and is secured with a wedge.

The hammer uses **leverage**: the further back you hold the handle, the more swing the head gets. That is why you hold it at the end of the handle when you want to strike hard. On impact, the head passes all its energy of movement to the nail in a short time. This creates a large force that drives the nail into the wood.

There are hammers for almost every job. The **claw hammer** has a split claw at the back for pulling out nails. The **rubber mallet** is soft and is used, for example, when laying tiles. The heavy sledgehammer is used for knocking down walls, and geologists use a special hammer to split rocks.

The blacksmith heats iron in the fire until it glows and becomes soft. Then he lays it on the **anvil**, a heavy block of steel, and shapes it with powerful hammer blows. In the past, horseshoes, tools, knives and railings were made like this. In Switzerland, at the Ballenberg open-air museum, you can still watch old craftsmen at work.

When hammering you wear safety glasses, because splinters of wood, stone or metal can fly into your eye. At the start you hold the nail with two fingers and strike lightly at first. As soon as it is in, you take your fingers away. A hammer with a loose head is dangerous and must be repaired.

Even in the Stone Age, people struck stones against other stones, bones or nuts. Later they fixed stones to wooden handles; these were the first real hammers. With the age of metals, hammers made of bronze and iron appeared. Today there are also machines that work on the hammer principle, such as the **pneumatic drill** on building sites.

begriffe.erklaerung: Heavy block of steel on which the blacksmith works metal.
A long lever makes a movement more powerful or faster.
Split end of the hammer head for pulling out nails.
Short, heavy hammer used, for example, for striking a chisel.

gewusst: In the human ear there are three tiny bones, and one of them is called the hammer.
In Norse legend the god Thor owns a magic hammer called Mjölnir.
In the hammer throw in athletics, a metal ball on a wire is hurled.

teile.einleitung: The Industrial Revolution was a huge upheaval that began in Great Britain around 1760. Machines, factories and steam power gradually replaced work by hand. People's lives changed more than at any time since the invention of farming.
wichtigste: The Industrial Revolution began in Great Britain in the 18th century.
The cotton industry is considered the first leading sector of industrialisation.
Steam engines, coke and iron made new machines and structures possible.
In 1830 the railway line between Liverpool and Manchester opened.
