Poverty, housing shortages and child labour were called the social question.
Early Swiss factories used mainly water power, because the country had hardly any coal.
The Swiss Federal Factory Act of 1877 introduced, among other things, the eleven-hour day.

abschnitte.text: The Industrial Revolution began in Great Britain, above all in the **cotton industry**. New spinning machines such as the spinning jenny and mechanical looms made yarn and cloth much faster than people could by hand. Instead of at home, people now worked in large **factories**. Great Britain had plenty of coal, iron ore, capital and a large sea trade. This made the country the pioneer.

In 1709 **Abraham Darby** in Coalbrookdale first used coke instead of charcoal to produce iron. This made it possible to make much more iron. In 1779 the **Iron Bridge** was built in Shropshire, the first large bridge made of cast iron. From 1769 James Watt made decisive improvements to the **steam engine**. Soon steam engines were driving pumps, looms and locomotives.

In 1830 the first intercity railway to run on a timetable with steam locomotives only was opened between **Liverpool and Manchester**. Railways carried goods and people much faster than horse-drawn carts. From England, industrialisation spread to Belgium, France, Germany and the USA. In Switzerland, the first railway running entirely within the country opened in 1847: the Spanisch-Brötli-Bahn from Zurich to Baden. The world moved closer together.

For many workers life was hard. They often worked 14 hours a day, and **children** also had to toil in factories. In the cities there were housing shortages, dirt and disease. These problems were called the **social question**. In 1845 Friedrich Engels described the hardship in his book “The Condition of the Working Class in England”.

Switzerland was one of the early industrial countries in Europe. Because there was hardly any coal, **water wheels** on rivers such as the Töss, Aabach or Limmat drove the first spinning mills. The textile industry was important, later engineering, watches and chemicals. As early as 1815 the Zurich government banned factory work for children under nine. The **Swiss Federal Factory Act** of 1877 brought the eleven-hour day and a ban on factory work for children under 14.

In the long run the Industrial Revolution brought more prosperity, better goods and new jobs. Workers joined together in **trade unions** and fought for better conditions. At the same time, humans began burning coal, and later oil, in large quantities. This is one cause of today's **climate change**. Our modern life with factories, trains and cities has its roots in this period.

begriffe.erklaerung: A large business in which goods are made with machines.
A fuel made from hard coal that burns very hot.
A branch of the economy that drives development.
The hardship of working people in the 19th century.
An association of employees that stands up for their rights.

gewusst: The Iron Bridge in England still stands today and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
The Spanisch-Brötli-Bahn got its name from a pastry from Baden that could be brought quickly to Zurich on it.
Before there were factories, many families in eastern Switzerland spun and wove at home as cottage industry.

teile.einleitung: Hydraulics is the technology of transmitting and multiplying forces with liquids. It makes use of the fact that liquids can hardly be squeezed together. Thanks to hydraulics, a digger can lift tonnes of earth and a car can be braked with light pressure on the pedal.
wichtigste: Hydraulics makes use of the fact that liquids can hardly be squeezed together.
Pressure spreads equally in all directions in a liquid, as Blaise Pascal discovered.
Hydraulic systems usually use oil.
In a hydraulic cylinder, the pressure of the liquid pushes a piston out.
A hydraulic press multiplies the force, but in return the distance at the small piston becomes longer.
1 bar equals 100,000 pascals.
Diggers usually move their arm with hydraulic cylinders.

abschnitte.text: The word hydraulics comes from Greek, where “hydor” means water. It refers to machines that transmit forces with a liquid. Because liquids can hardly be squeezed together, a liquid passes on any pressure immediately. If air is used instead of a liquid, it is called **pneumatics**.

In the 17th century the French scientist **Blaise Pascal** discovered that pressure in an enclosed liquid spreads equally in all directions. Pressure is force divided by area. In his honour, the unit of pressure is called the **pascal**. One bar is 100,000 pascals, which is about the air pressure at sea level.

A **hydraulic press** has a small and a large piston connected by liquid. If you press on the small piston of 2 square centimetres with 50 newtons, a force of 2,500 newtons acts on the large piston of 100 square centimetres. The area is 50 times bigger, so the force is too. But in return you have to push the small piston 50 times further than the large one moves, because energy cannot be gained.

A **pump** puts the liquid under pressure, often several hundred bar. Hoses and pipes carry it to where it is used, and valves control where it flows. In the **hydraulic cylinder**, the liquid pushes a piston out. **Oil** is usually used, because it lubricates the parts at the same time and protects them from rust.

Diggers, cranes, tractors and dustcarts move their arms with hydraulic cylinders. The brakes of a car also work hydraulically; the foot presses on the brake pads via brake fluid. In garages, hydraulic lifts raise whole cars. The landing gear of aircraft and many bike brakes also use hydraulics.

begriffe.erklaerung: Force acting on a certain area.
Movable part in a cylinder that is pushed by the liquid.
Unit of pressure, named after Blaise Pascal.
Technology that transmits forces with compressed air instead of liquid.

gewusst: With a hydraulic press, a person can move loads as heavy as a car using little force.
The Englishman Joseph Bramah patented the hydraulic press in the 18th century.
A digger can control several hydraulic cylinders at once so that the boom, arm and bucket move together.

teile.einleitung: A smart grid is a power grid in which generation, storage and consumption are coordinated using communication technology. It helps to make good use of electricity from sun and wind, even though this is not always produced evenly. Smart electricity meters, batteries and controlled appliances are important building blocks of it.
wichtigste: In a smart grid, generation, storage and consumption are coordinated using communication technology.
According to the Electricity Supply Ordinance, Swiss grid operators must replace 80 per cent of meters with smart meters by the end of 2027.
A prosumer uses electricity and also produces electricity themselves, for example with a solar system.
Load management deliberately shifts consumption to times when plenty is available.
A virtual power station is a group of many small installations that are controlled together.
For decades Swiss grid operators have switched electric water heaters on and off centrally using ripple control.
Decentralised installations feeding into lower grid levels make running the grid more demanding.
With digitalisation, the risk of cyber attacks on the control technology grows.

abschnitte.text: In the past electricity flowed almost only in one direction: from large power stations along lines to homes. In a **smart grid**, power stations, storage and consumers constantly exchange data. In this way the grid knows where and how much electricity is being produced and used at any moment. The aim is that exactly as much electricity is always fed into the grid as is used.

Today many Swiss roofs have **solar panels** that feed electricity into the grid. Someone who uses electricity and also produces it is called a **prosumer**, a word mixed from producer and consumer. Because this electricity is fed into lower grid levels, it sometimes flows in the opposite direction from before. In addition, the sun does not always shine, and at midday there is often more electricity than is needed at that moment.

A **smart meter** is a digital electricity meter that measures consumption precisely and sends the data automatically. In Switzerland, according to the Electricity Supply Ordinance, grid operators must have replaced 80 per cent of meters by the end of 2027. This lets households see more precisely when they use how much electricity. Grid operators can then plan the grid better.

With **load management**, consumption is shifted to times when plenty of electricity is available. Examples are electric water heaters, heat pumps or electric cars that run or charge when a lot of solar power is being produced. In Switzerland there has long been **ripple control** for this: signals sent over the power grid switch water heaters on and off centrally. Modern systems do this much more finely and quickly.

Many small installations such as solar roofs, batteries and combined heat and power units can be linked together to form a **virtual power station**. Central software then controls them together like one large power station. Pumped storage power stations in the Alps also help to store electricity and release it when needed. In future, electric car batteries could also feed electricity back into the grid.

Because many devices are networked in a smart grid, the risk of **cyber attacks** on the control technology rises. A successful attack could, in the worst case, lead to power cuts. That is why data must be encrypted and systems well protected. Data protection is also important, because consumption data reveals a lot about everyday life in a household.

begriffe.erklaerung: An intelligent power grid, “intelligentes Stromnetz” in German.
Digital electricity meter that sends data automatically.
Someone who uses electricity and also produces electricity themselves.
Deliberately shifting electricity use to favourable times.
Older technology that switches appliances centrally using signals in the power grid.

gewusst: Many Swiss electric water heaters have heated mainly at night for decades, because ripple control switches them on then.
On sunny middays, some European countries can have so much solar power that the electricity price on the exchange drops below zero.
An electric car with a full battery could supply a family house with electricity for several days.

teile.einleitung: Hans Hilfiker was a Swiss engineer and designer. In 1944 he designed the famous SBB station clock, which is now seen as a symbol of Swiss punctuality. He also helped to set the dimensions of Swiss kitchens.
wichtigste: Hans Hilfiker was born in Zurich in 1901 and died in 1993.
He studied electrical engineering at ETH Zurich.
In 1944 he designed the well-known SBB station clock.
The red second hand recalls the signalling disc of the stationmaster.
At every full minute the second hand stops for about 1.5 seconds.
Hilfiker helped shape the Swiss kitchen standard with appliances 55 centimetres wide.
From 1958 he was director of the Glarus company Therma.

abschnitte.text: Hans Hilfiker was born in **Zurich** in 1901. He studied electrical engineering at **ETH Zurich** and became an engineer. Later he worked for the Swiss Federal Railways, SBB. There he looked after technical equipment in stations, for example clocks and lighting.

In 1944 Hilfiker designed the **SBB station clock**, with a white face, black bars instead of numbers and black hands. It is easy to read even from a long way off. Later the red **second hand** with the round disc was added. It recalls the signalling disc with which the stationmaster gave a train the signal to depart.

The second hand takes only about 58.5 seconds to go round once. Then it stops at the top, at twelve, for about 1.5 seconds. It waits for an electrical pulse from a central **master clock**, which then makes the minute hand jump forward one step. In this way all the clocks in the stations run exactly the same, and trains can leave on time.

Hilfiker also worked on kitchens. He helped to develop the **Swiss kitchen standard**, according to which cookers, fridges and cupboards are 55 centimetres wide. This means appliances from different makers fit into every kitchen. From 1958 he ran the company **Therma** in Schwanden in the canton of Glarus as its director; it made kitchen appliances.

Today the station clock is considered a classic of Swiss design and hangs in museums. Since the 1980s the watch company Mondaine has sold wristwatches in this style. In 2012 an American technology company used the design in an app. According to media reports, it then paid the SBB about 20 million francs.

begriffe.erklaerung: Central clock that gives the exact time to many other clocks.
In the past, the head of a station, who gave trains the signal to depart.
Shaping objects so that they are attractive and practical.
A rule that sets how big something should be or how it should be built.

gewusst: Hans Hilfiker's station clock does not have a single number on its face.
The 55-centimetre kitchen standard applies in Switzerland, while 60 centimetres is usual in many European countries.
The brief pause of the second hand looks as if the clock is taking a breath.

teile.einleitung: Industry 4.0 describes factories in which machines, workpieces and computers are connected with each other via the internet. The machines constantly exchange data and can partly control themselves. The number 4.0 stands for the idea that this is seen as the fourth industrial revolution.
wichtigste: Industry 4.0 means networking machines, sensors and workpieces in the factory.
The term was presented to a wide public at the Hannover Messe trade fair in 2011.
In English it is also called the Industrial Internet of Things.
A digital twin is a virtual copy of a real machine with its real-time data.
Predictive maintenance uses sensor data to recognise when a machine is about to fail.
Cobots are robots that work directly with people without a safety fence.
The goal of “batch size 1” means making one-off items as cheaply as mass-produced goods.

abschnitte.text: The number recalls the version numbers of software. The **first industrial revolution** brought steam engines and mechanical looms from the 18th century. The second followed with electricity and the assembly line. The third brought computers and automation from the 1970s. The **fourth** now connects all machines via the internet.

abschnitte.titel: Machines that talk to each other
abschnitte.text: In a networked factory, machines have many **sensors** that measure, for example, temperature, pressure or vibrations. Such systems made of mechanics, sensors and software are called **cyber-physical systems**. So that machines from different makers understand each other, shared languages such as the **OPC UA** standard are needed. For wireless connections, 5G mobile communication is considered important because of its very short delays. Even a workpiece can carry a chip that tells the machine how it should be processed.

A **digital twin** is an exact copy of a machine or a whole factory in the computer. It is constantly fed with the real measurement data. In this way changes can first be tried out on the computer before they are put into practice in the real factory. Engineers can see on the screen how every machine is doing. As a result, faults can be spotted earlier.

In the past, machines were maintained according to fixed schedules or only when they broke down. With **predictive maintenance**, computers analyse the sensor data. If a bearing, for example, vibrates more than usual, the system reports that it is about to fail. Then the part can be replaced in good time. This saves money and prevents the whole production line from standing still.

**Collaborative robots**, cobots for short, work right next to people without a safety fence. They sense when they touch a person and stop immediately. A cobot can, for example, hold heavy parts while a person assembles them. A big goal of Industry 4.0 is **batch size 1**: every product can be individual and still be made cheaply. Many Swiss companies, for example in the engineering and watch industries, are also relying on such networked factories.

begriffe.erklaerung: A measuring probe that detects, for example, heat, pressure or movement.
A virtual copy of a real machine in the computer.
A robot that works closely with people.
Maintenance that predicts failures from data.
The number of identical items made in one run.

gewusst: With Industry 4.0, a customer can put their product together online, and the factory makes exactly that one item.
The term Industry 4.0 comes from Germany and is often simply taken over in English.
A cobot can be programmed by a person simply showing it a movement by guiding its arm.

teile.einleitung: A hand mixer is an electric kitchen appliance that you hold in your hand and use to mix dough, beat egg whites or whip cream. Two fast-turning beaters do in a few minutes what would take a lot of strength and time by hand. It is part of the basic equipment of many Swiss kitchens.
wichtigste: A hand mixer is an electric mixing device that you hold in your hand.
It usually has two beaters that turn against each other.
A hand mixer is the fastest way to whip cream.
For heavy doughs there are special dough hooks.
The speed can be set in several stages.
When whipping, a lot of air is beaten into the cream or egg white.
Before inserting or changing the beaters, you must pull out the plug.

abschnitte.text: A hand mixer consists of a casing with a handle, an **electric motor** and two openings for the attachments. The motor drives the two **beaters** via gearwheels, and they turn in opposite directions. You can usually choose three to five speeds. Unlike a **food processor**, you hold the hand mixer yourself and move it through the bowl.

When whipping cream, the beaters stir lots of tiny **air bubbles** into the liquid. The fat droplets in the cream gather around the bubbles and hold them in place. In this way liquid cream turns into an airy, firm mass, **whipped cream**. It works best with well-chilled cream, and you should not whip it for too long, otherwise it turns into butter.

The normal wire **beaters** are suitable for cream, beaten egg whites, creams and runny batters such as cake mixture. For heavy doughs, such as bread or plaited loaf dough, you use spiral-shaped **dough hooks**. Some devices also have a blender stick as an attachment. Egg whites can only be beaten until stiff if there is no yolk and no fat in the bowl.

In the past everything was mixed by hand with a **whisk**, which took a lot of strength and stamina. At the beginning of the 20th century the first electric mixers appeared in the USA, at first as large stand machines for bakeries. Later the devices became smaller, lighter and cheaper. From the middle of the 20th century, hand mixers found their way into many households, including in Switzerland.

The beaters turn very fast and can catch fingers, hair or cables. That is why you only insert or change the beaters when the **plug is pulled out**. You start on a slow setting so that nothing splashes out of the bowl. Children should first use the hand mixer together with an adult.

begriffe.erklaerung: An attachment made of bent wire that beats air into liquids as it turns.
A spiral-shaped attachment for kneading heavy dough.
A motor that converts electrical energy into rotation.
Cream that has become light and firm by being beaten with air.

gewusst: If you whip cream for too long, it turns into butter.
The two beaters of a hand mixer turn in opposite directions.
Cream roughly doubles in volume when whipped, because a lot of air gets into it.

teile.einleitung: Josephine Cochrane was an American inventor who built the first practical dishwasher. In 1886 she received a patent for it. Her idea still makes work in the kitchen easier for millions of people today.
wichtigste: Josephine Cochrane invented the dishwasher.
In 1886 she received the patent for her machine.
She got the idea because her valuable china was damaged during washing up.
In her machine, soapy water sprayed from nozzles onto wire baskets holding the dishes.
In 1893 she presented the machine at the World's Fair in Chicago.
At first it was mainly hotels and restaurants that bought her machines.
She lived and worked in the USA.
Her great-grandfather John Fitch is known for an early steamboat.

abschnitte.text: Josephine Cochrane was born in 1839 in the state of **Ohio** in the USA and died in Chicago in 1913. Her father was an engineer, and her great-grandfather **John Fitch** had built an early steamboat back in the 18th century. She married a wealthy man and lived in Illinois. She liked to invite guests and used her valuable china for them.

When washing up by hand, plates and cups from her precious china kept getting broken. Cochrane was annoyed by this and wanted a machine that washed faster and more gently. After her husband's death in 1883 she was also in debt and needed money. So she began to put her idea into practice in earnest.

Cochrane measured every piece of china exactly and built matching **wire baskets** for plates, cups and saucers. The baskets sat on a wheel in a boiler. While the wheel turned, hot **soapy water** sprayed from nozzles onto the dishes. A mechanic helped her build it, and in 1886 she received the **patent**.

At the **World's Fair in Chicago** in 1893, Cochrane presented her machine to a huge audience. Restaurants on the exhibition grounds used it to wash their dishes, and the invention won an award. After that it was mainly **hotels and restaurants** that ordered the machines, because they were too big and too expensive for normal households. She founded her own company to make the machines.

Only from the middle of the 20th century did dishwashers become common in private households too. Today most Swiss kitchens have a dishwasher, often in the Swiss standard width of 55 centimetres. Modern machines often use less water than washing up by hand. Over several stages, Cochrane's company later became a well-known American brand of kitchen appliances.

begriffe.erklaerung: A right that secures an invention for its inventor for a certain time.
Large international exhibition at which countries show new inventions.
Narrow opening from which water or air sprays out under pressure.
Fine, white and valuable material for crockery.

gewusst: Josephine Cochrane is said to have declared that if nobody else would invent a dishwasher, she would do it herself.
Her family name was actually spelt Cochran; she added the e at the end herself.
In 2006 Cochrane was inducted into the American National Inventors Hall of Fame.

teile.einleitung: A high-rise building is a building with very many storeys that reaches far up into the sky. Especially tall ones are called skyscrapers. The tallest building in Switzerland is the Roche Tower Building 2 in Basel.
wichtigste: A high-rise is a building with many storeys.
Very tall high-rises are called skyscrapers.
High-rises are built mainly where there is little space in cities.
The tallest building in the world is in Dubai (as of 2025).

abschnitte.text: In big cities land is scarce and expensive. If you build upwards, you can fit many **flats** and offices onto a small area. The individual levels are called **storeys**. The district of **Manhattan** in New York is famous for its many high-rises. Cities such as Hong Kong, Shanghai and Dubai also have impressive skylines.

High-rises only became possible when two inventions came together. A **steel frame** carries the weight, so the walls no longer have to support everything. And safe **lifts** carry people up comfortably; Elisha Otis presented the first safety device against lifts falling in the 1850s. The Home Insurance Building in Chicago of 1885 is considered one of the first skyscrapers. In 1931 the Empire State Building was completed in New York, and for a long time it was the tallest building in the world.

A very tall high-rise **sways** a little in strong wind; this is normal and intended. Some towers have heavy pendulums at the top that dampen the swaying. For emergencies every high-rise needs a protected **stairwell** as an escape route, because lifts must not be used in a fire. There are also sprinkler systems and fire walls. Red lights on the roof warn aeroplanes and helicopters at night.

The tallest building in the world is the **Burj Khalifa** in Dubai, which opened in 2010. It is 828 metres tall, more than twice as tall as the Eiffel Tower in Paris. Most skyscrapers today are being built in Asia and the Middle East. Many countries compete to own the tallest building. Records often last only a few years, until a new tower is even taller.

In Switzerland a building counts as a high-rise from about 25 to 30 metres, depending on the canton. The tallest building is the **Roche Tower Building 2** in Basel at 205 metres, which was completed in 2022. Next to it stands the slightly smaller Building 1 from 2015. In Zurich the **Prime Tower** at 126 metres is well known. For a long time relatively few high-rises were built in Switzerland, but today more are being built because people want to save building land.

teile.einleitung: A cable is a line that carries electricity, signals or data from one place to another. Inside there are metal wires or glass fibres, and outside a plastic sheath protects them. Cables are everywhere, but you have to be careful with electricity, because a damaged cable can be deadly.
wichtigste: A cable carries electricity, signals or data.
The plastic sheath protects against electric shocks.
A device with a damaged cable must not be used any more.
Cables should not be laid under carpets or trapped in doors, because they can be damaged and overheat.
A cable reel must be fully unwound before you connect a powerful appliance.
Tall pylons carry the power lines across the country.
Near power lines and overhead railway lines there is a danger to life.

abschnitte.text: Inside, a power cable usually has several **cores** made of copper, because copper conducts electricity very well. Each core is insulated with plastic so that the wires do not touch. On the outside there is a further plastic sheath, the **insulation**, which protects against electric shocks and damage. In Switzerland the protective earth conductor is green and yellow, the neutral conductor blue and the live conductor usually brown.

Besides power cables there are cables for data, such as network cables, USB cables or aerial cables. Modern **fibre-optic cables** transmit data as light signals through wafer-thin glass fibres. Huge submarine cables lie on the sea floor and connect continents for the internet. The first telegraph cable across the Atlantic was laid as early as 1858, but it only worked for a few weeks.

High-voltage lines carry electricity from power stations over long distances. They hang on tall frames, the **pylons**. Some lines are also laid as underground cables. Above the SBB tracks hangs the **overhead line**, at a voltage of 15,000 volts, which supplies the trains with electricity.

A damaged cable where you can see the wires can cause an **electric shock**, so you stop using the device. Cables under carpets or trapped in doors get squashed and can overheat and start a fire. Never fly kites near power lines. Climbing onto stationary railway wagons is deadly dangerous, because electricity can jump across from the overhead line over a distance.

With an **extension cable**, a device can stand further away from the socket. A cable reel must be fully unwound before you connect a powerful appliance such as a fan heater, otherwise it can get hot. Always pull the plug and not the cable when unplugging a device. Cables should not be kinked or laid over sharp edges.
